French presidential hopeful Teddy Riner says Ukraine is ‘not our war’
articles.summary: The Olympic gold medalist’s remarks on Russia’s ongoing full-scale invasion provoked a backlash
articles.body: The Olympic gold medalist’s remarks on Russia’s ongoing full-scale invasion provoked a backlash. PARIS — Teddy Riner, the legendary judoka running for president in France, sparked controversy on Wednesday after declaring that Ukraine was not his country's conflict. "I don't understand why we're sending troops to Ukraine when it's not our war," the five-time Olympic gold medalist told reporters . Riner was referring to the deployment of French troops in Ukraine, which was criticized by opposition parties for having been decided without parliamentary approval. Deputy Defense Minister Alice Rufo said the troops are "dedicated to training and equipment maintenance." "If I become president tomorrow, I would like to be the kind of person who brings people together, who smiles and shakes hands to put an end to this war," Riner added about Russia's war in Ukraine. Russian leader Vladimir Putin also practices judo and was honorary president of the International Judo Federation before launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The 37-year-old Riner has unveiled few policy proposals and had not yet weighed in on foreign affairs since announcing his candidacy earlier this month . The two leading candidates for next April's election in France — far-right chief Marine Le Pen and far-left veteran Jean-Luc Mélenchon — have both been critical of current President Emmanuel Macron's Ukraine policy. Macron's government has sent funds and weapons to Ukraine and co-led the coalition of the willing, a group of Kyiv's most significant allies and supporters. Riner, however, had been more closely associated with the pro-Macron camp based on early campaign statements, making his Ukraine comments more surprising. Early surveys have shown him polling at about 4%, drawing mostly from voters who opted for Macron in the last presidential election. Center-right MEP Nathalie Loiseau, who handles foreign affairs policy for presidential candidate Edouard Philippe, seized on Riner's remarks to attack the election rival. "Teddy Riner's world would be so simple: you don't get involved in anything, you shake hands with everyone, and there's peace and love all over the world," she wrote on X . Riner was speaking from the French mayors' congress currently taking place in Paris, where he was seeking out endorsements needed to run for president. He still has a long way to go before actually getting onto the ballot: Riner said he had obtained more than 100 signatures from local officials in support his candidacy — far from the 500 needed to confirm his candidacy under French law.

articles.title: Five Russian military jets hit in airfield strike, says Ukraine
articles.summary: Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow
articles.body: Ukraine has said it damaged five Russian military aircraft in an attack on Russia's Savasleyka airfield, 300km (185 miles) east of Moscow. Three MiG-31 and two Su-34s aircraft were hit, Kyiv's General Staff said, adding that the extent of the damage was still being assessed but that "there may be even better news to come". It did not elaborate on what weapons it had used to hit the airfield. The airfield at Savasleyka, in Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region, has been a target for Ukraine for several years. It hosts aircraft used by Russia to launch hypersonic missiles and glide bombs. The take-off of MiG-31s in particular frequently triggers nationwide alerts across Ukraine, as the Kinzhal missiles they carry have been known to hit large infrastructure and military targets and are difficult to shoot down. Overnight, Kyiv also said it hit two oil refineries in Russia's Samara region some 800km (500 miles) from the front line – the latest in a series of long-range strikes which have dented Moscow's oil processing capacity. "Did you repair them? We'll hit them again," the defence ministry in Kyiv said. Samara region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev said the night-time attacks had been "a true ordeal", with more than 145 drones shot down. One person was killed and several towns experienced power outages, Fedorishchev said. Kyiv also said it had hit a radar system as well as fuel and logistics depots across Ukrainian territories currently occupied by Russia. "Without fuel, military vehicles cannot move; without ammunition, artillery falls silent," the defence ministry said, adding that every successful hit meant Moscow could carry out fewer strikes. Kyiv has developed a thriving weapons industry and Ukrainian strikes on Russian targets well beyond the front line have become commonplace in the years since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion. On Tuesday, President Vladimir Putin called for a tightening of security measures across the country's energy facilities. But he also argued that Russia had managed to stabilise its domestic fuel market without suffering "critical damage" and added that Moscow would "inevitably" retaliate against Kyiv. Ukraine continues to come under daily attack. Ten people were killed across several regions between 24 and 25 November, while thousands are without power after Russian strikes on energy infrastructure.

Russian sources say Europeans must take up Putin's offer for Moscow talks
articles.body:
Numerous sources inside Russian foreign policy circles on Wednesday underscored the Kremlin's desire for European diplomats to travel to Moscow and explain their intentions before they be allowed to participate in any Russia-Ukraine peace negotiations.

Russian President Vladimir Putin originally extended the invitation last month. On Wednesday, Foreign Policy Advisor Yury Ushakov said the invitation stands but that no Europeans have so far agreed to embark on the diplomatic sojourn.

Russia's Ambassador to Germany Sergei Nechayev on Wednesday told France's AFP news agency that reaction to Putin's invitation has been "restrained."

Nechayev claimed that Moscow remains, "ready to continue the dialogue and carry on with negotiations."

He also repeated the Kremlin claim that it is Europe that is the impediment to stopping the war, and that Russia — which launched and continues to execute its unprovoked years-long war of aggression in Ukraine — is the only party truly interested in peace.

Nechayev said the Kremlin doesn't see the same "honesty" from the Europeans that it does from US President Donald Trump's team — made up of his son-in-law Jared Kushner and his friend Steve Witkoff — and wants to "know precisely what their intentions are."

Russia has been accused of foot dragging as a way to prolong attacks on Ukraine. On Wednesday, Nechayev continued in that vein, saying: "Our request to Europe is this: Decide what it is you want, determine whom you will appoint as negotiators, and, most importantly, clarify what you aim to achieve."

“Burchuladze and other political prisoners must be released” – European Parliament draft resolution
articles.summary: Debates on a draft resolution concerning Georgia will be held in the European Parliament on November 25
articles.body: Debates on a draft resolution concerning Georgia will be held in the European Parliament on November 25. The resolution concerns the case of Paata Burchuladze and political prisoners under the Georgian Dream government. The vote is scheduled for November 26. The document calls for the immediate and unconditional release of all political prisoners and unlawfully detained individuals, regardless of their political affiliation. Those named in the resolution include Paata Burchuladze, Irakli Nadiradze, and Paata Manjgaladze. The authors of a draft resolution in the European Parliament describe the charges against Paata Burchuladze as politically motivated. The 71-year-old opera singer and civil activist was sentenced to seven years in prison in May 2026. The so-called “peaceful overthrow” case is linked to a protest held in Tbilisi on October 4, 2025. Burchuladze denies the charges. The resolution’s authors question the fairness of the trial and the proportionality of the sentence. They also raise concerns about Burchuladze’s prolonged isolation, strict restrictions on contact with the outside world and inadequate medical care. The authors call on the Georgian authorities to ensure that Burchuladze receives appropriate medical and legal assistance and is allowed regular contact with his family. The document also states that Burchuladze, who holds Georgian and Austrian citizenship, should be able to meet consular representatives without obstruction. The resolution’s authors reiterate their call for the EU to impose targeted sanctions and visa bans on individuals responsible for serious human rights violations. The document names Bidzina Ivanishvili, Irakli Kobakhidze, Shalva Papuashvili and Kakha Kaladze. The call also extends to other senior officials, as well as judges, prosecutors and law enforcement officers. The authors say Burchuladze’s case should be viewed in the context of democratic backsliding in Georgia, the weakening of judicial independence and Russia’s growing influence. They argue that Georgian Dream is using the judiciary and other state institutions to suppress dissent. The resolution’s authors call on the Georgian authorities to end the politically motivated persecution of artists, opposition figures, journalists and activists. They also demand independent investigations into reports of excessive force against protesters, intimidation and ill-treatment. The document stresses that progress toward EU membership requires respect for the rule of law, the European Convention on Human Rights, and fundamental rights. articles.summary: Joint military exercises between Belarus and Russia were held in the Brest and Gomel regions
articles.body: Belarus is not involved in the attack on Ukraine and did not provide Russia with any bases to carry out attacks, states self-proclaimed President of Belarus Alexander Lukashenko.I specifically took a map of Belarus so that you could understand. Joint military exercises between Belarus and Russia were held in the Brest and Gomel regions. These were scheduled exercises in 2022. After their completion, Russian troops were supposed to leave Belarusian territory, he said. Lukashenko noted that the US had warned that war might begin and informed Ukraine about troop concentrations near the borders, adding that he did not believe such a thing could happen. The Russians began withdrawing their troops by rail and road. The troops from Brest were withdrawn, but those remaining in other areas somehow turned toward Kyiv and decided to advance through it. I have absolutely no connection to the start of the war, he emphasized. He claimed he was unaware of the war's commencement and that the Russian General Staff did not inform him about it. You may ask why I didn't intervene and stop the Russians. But why should I have stopped them and fought for Ukraine? Ukraine was already at war with Belarus, Lukashenko said. In particular, he recalled the imposition of sanctions against Minsk, the closure of airspace, and the seizure of wagons. So why should I have defended Ukraine when the war started? Everyone knows we have no connection to this war. We do not want war; we do not need it, the self-proclaimed president summarized. In March 2022, during a meeting with Russian leader Vladimir Putin, Lukashenko brought a map which, according to him, was meant to confirm Ukraine's alleged preparation for an attack on Russian and Belarusian troops stationed in Belarus during joint exercises. Lukashenko claimed that the Armed Forces of Ukraine planned to attack four positions, and that a preemptive Russian strike allegedly prevented this. However, he provided no evidence for his accusations. Furthermore, in July 2023, Lukashenko boasted of a map on which one could allegedly see the transfer of Polish troops to the borders of Belarus.

articles.summary: The head of the "Serbia Wins" parliamentary group, Aleksandar Vucic, said today that the arrest of the editor-in-chief of Informer, Dragan J
articles.body: The head of the "Serbia Wins" parliamentary group, Aleksandar Vucic, said today that the arrest of the editor-in-chief of Informer, Dragan J. Vucicevic , is an incredibly brazen acts unseen in Serbia before, and asserted that Vucicevic is fighting for his ideas. "In front of me is the decision on the detention of Dragan J. Vucicevic. This was done with the approval of the prosecutor from the Second Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, Marko Pljakic, against Dragan Vucicevic, for allegedly obstructing justice and causing panic and unrest. This is incredibly insolent," Vucic said in a video posted on the Instagram account "avucic". He added that the decision states that Informer (TV) has national frequency, which he said is not true. "That the night when they broke into his television, they said that 'the suspect, using the platform of Informer TV, which has national internet frequency' - they are spouting nonsense, (Informer) doesn't have national frequency, but revolutionary prosecutors are allowed. But, pay attention: 'In the extended period from 2023 to 2026, he systematically carried out a media campaign of spreading hatred, intolerance and public targeting'," quoted Vucic. He added that they are further announcing that the biggest problem is that Vucicevic said that a Maidan, the civil war and a car full of gasoline are being prepared. "They were preparing both a Maidan and the civil war. They had cars, I don't know if they were full of gasoline, but they were full of knives, clubs, drugs, and everything else. They had all that. Well, such bandits, the prosecutors, these kind of servants of the newly established criminal regime, whose drug and armed wing is the Vracar Clan, we have never seen anything like this," said Vucic. Vucic pointed out that Vucicevic refused to sign receiving the decision and that on the line, below which it read, "The decision was received by Dragan Vucicevic", instead of his signature, the Informer editor-in-chief wrote, "I refuse to sign, this is political persecution". "It was rightly written by him, and he showed once again how brave he is and how much he fights for his ideas. Serbia has never experienced something like this," said Vucic. He asked whether, when it comes to prosecution and lies, those who lied about the sound cannon, Jovanjica, Sarajevo safari, a boy allegedly killed in Valjevo are being prosecuted, and stated that they are not. "Servants always have their price and luckily they always show themselves as such. Well, the whole world has now seen and the whole of Serbia has seen what they have turned our country into, and Dragan J. Vucicevic will persevere, he will endure the terror of the majority in a parliament that applauds (his arrest) with abandon, in front of his son, apparently rejoicing in another's misfortune," said Vucic. Vucic also stated that those holding him are not allowing Vucicevic to take his medication until they receive a doctor's report that he should be taking those medications. "This kind of gang has never been in power anywhere, in any European country. Never. That's fine. We will fight," said Vucic. The editor-in-chief of Informer, Dragan J. Vucicevic, was arrested this morning by order of the Second Basic Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade on suspicion of having committed the prolonged criminal offense of causing unrest and panic and the criminal offense of obstruction of justice.

articles.title: BiH Needs Democratic Constitutional Reform, Not ‘Special Treatment,’ Professor Says
articles.summary: David Pettigrew of Southern Connecticut State University
articles.body: Thirty-one years after the signing of the Dayton Peace Agreement, Bosnia and Herzegovina needs democratic constitutional reform and stronger support from the European Union (EU), rather than what has been described as “special treatment,” according to Professor Dr. David Pettigrew of Southern Connecticut State University. In an opinion piece marking the anniversary of the Dayton Agreement, Pettigrew, a professor and Chairperson of the Philosophy Department, argued that the current constitutional framework is increasingly being used to accommodate ethnonationalist interests, while preventing meaningful democratic reform. He warned that separatist agendas pursued by Bosnian Serb and Bosnian Croat ethnonationalists continue to destabilize Bosnia and Herzegovina and the wider region, while the Dayton Peace Agreement has become an excuse for political inaction. Referring to remarks made by EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos on November 5, Pettigrew highlighted her assessment that existing EU methodologies and financial instruments for candidate countries are not working effectively for Bosnia and Herzegovina. “No methodology we have for the candidate countries and no financial instrument we have for the candidate countries is working for Bosnia and Herzegovina,” Kos stated, adding that the EU would need to consider developing a special approach for the country after the elections. Pettigrew questioned what such an approach would entail, stressing that the EU must not act as a passive observer while political and institutional challenges continue to deepen. He argued that decades of insufficient engagement by the international community and the EU have contributed directly to the current situation, despite obligations under Bosnia and Herzegovina’s Stabilization and Association Agreement. The agreement commits the EU to supporting the country’s political, economic and institutional stabilization, as well as the development of civil society and democratization. It also emphasizes respect for human rights, the rule of law and democratic principles. However, Pettigrew believes that the EU has failed to adequately support constitutional reforms necessary to guarantee these principles, including the implementation of judgments issued by the European Court of Human Rights. In particular, he pointed to the Sejdić-Finci and Zornić judgments, which address discrimination within Bosnia and Herzegovina’s constitutional and electoral system. The European Court of Human Rights found that restrictions based on ethnicity and the constitutional concept of constituent peoples result in discrimination incompatible with democratic standards. Rather than working more closely with citizens’ organizations, including KRUG 99, to promote a constitutional system based on equality among citizens, Pettigrew argued that the EU’s inaction has contributed to the strengthening of ethnic divisions and nationalist ideologies. He also warned that the glorification of convicted war criminals and individuals implicated in wartime atrocities represents a serious obstacle to reconciliation and transitional justice. As an example, he cited the statue erected in Nevesinje in 2020 in honour of Novica Gušić, a Bosnian Serb commander whom he described as implicated in the murder of civilians, including children. Pettigrew also referred to the public funeral held in Serbia in September for Ratko Mladić, who was convicted of genocide and other war crimes, noting that the ceremony included military honours. According to the professor, monuments and public ceremonies celebrating individuals associated with genocide and other war crimes undermine efforts to establish transitional justice and should prompt a decisive response from the international community and the EU. Concluding his remarks on the anniversary of the Dayton Agreement, Pettigrew stressed that Bosnia and Herzegovina does not need special treatment, but rather consistent international support for the development of a functioning constitutional democracy. Such a system, he argued, should guarantee equality among all citizens, protect human rights and ensure the rule of law. Prof. Dr. David Pettigrew is a Professor and Chairperson of the Philosophy Department at Southern Connecticut State University.

The Limits of Illiberal Power: What the Defeats of Vucic and Orban Reveal
articles.summary: The similarities are striking, but so are the differences
articles.body: Within just a few months, two of Europe’s most entrenched political leaders, Viktor Orban in Hungary and Aleksandar Vucic in Serbia, lost power after more than a decade of increasingly authoritarian rule. In both countries, new opposition movements succeeded where their predecessors had failed for years, mobilising voters beyond traditional urban opposition strongholds and into smaller towns and rural areas long dominated by the governing parties. The similarities are striking, but so are the differences. Hungary’s opposition was led by Peter Magyar, a former government insider who built a highly centralised party, Tisza. Serbia’s emerged from a decentralised student protest movement that eventually formed an electoral alternative, the Student List. While both governments systematically captured state resources, political intimidation and violence was considerably more prominent under Vucic than under Orban. Yet both movements united voters across ideological divides and defeated seemingly unbeatable governments. Why did they succeed where their predecessors had failed? Economic difficulties, political scandals, government fatigue and changes in the media environment all contributed. But the comparison suggests that the most important transformation took place on the other side of politics – the opposition itself. There is some evidence that Hungarian and Serbian societies have become more liberal, particularly among younger voters. Yet research suggests that neither victory reflected a fundamental ideological transformation. In Hungary , liberal identification increased without fundamentally reshaping the country’s ideological landscape. Similarly, Serbia’s student movement attracted both pro-European and nationalist opposition voters, despite their persistent ideological differences. Both movements deliberately avoided presenting themselves as ideological alternatives to every aspect of the governments that they challenged. Magyar’s Tisza embraced national symbols and adopted Fidesz’s position on immigration, appealing to former government supporters as well as traditional opposition voters. Serbia’s students similarly avoided divisive questions such as Kosovo. Neither made progressive social policies or liberal values central to their campaigns. Instead, both united voters around a simpler promise: removing the existing government. Their success suggests that defeating an illiberal government does not necessarily require rejecting all the values it represents. Indeed, embracing some of those values may be essential to winning over its former supporters. For years, Hungary and Serbia were characterised by fragmented and discredited opposition parties that struggled to challenge the governments beyond major cities. Successive elections saw them compete for a limited electorate, while failing to convince voters that they offered a credible alternative to the governing parties. Tisza and the Student List broke with this pattern. Neither carried the political baggage of repeated electoral defeats or years of participation in a political system that many voters had come to distrust. They could therefore present themselves as a clear break with the existing order. Both movements also understood that their supporters were primarily dissatisfied with the political system itself, rather than with particular government policies. Their campaigns focused less on ideological disputes and more on defeating the incumbents and putting their countries ‘back on the right track’. Mass demonstrations, marches and direct challenges to the governments’ legitimacy became central to their political identity. Although earlier opposition parties had also protested corruption, their continued participation in the political system made it harder for them to represent a genuine break with it. Tisza and the Student List instead presented the elections as a choice between preserving the existing order and bringing it to an end. Perhaps most importantly, they gave voters a reason to believe that victory was actually possible. There was also something distinctly populist about their approach: they appealed to widespread frustration with the ruling political elite rather than offering a clearly defined alternative ideology. Yet the two movements differed considerably in their organisation. Tisza developed into a highly centralised, professionalised party centred around Magyar’s leadership, while Serbia’s Student List emerged from a decentralised movement based on grassroots decision-making. Their shared success therefore cannot be attributed to one particular organisational model. What mattered more was their novelty, their ability to mobilise beyond established opposition circles, and their determination to win. While the opposition’s transformation was crucial, the governments they faced had also become considerably more vulnerable. By 2026, Orban’s Fidesz had ruled Hungary for 16 years and Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) for 14. Over time, grievances, scandals and dissatisfaction accumulated, even among former government supporters. Long incumbency also became a liability: after more than a decade, it became increasingly difficult to blame previous governments or outside forces for economic problems, deteriorating public services or corruption. Economic conditions compounded these pressures. In Hungary, years of growth gave way to stagnation and high inflation, which reached 17.6 per cent in 2023, the highest in the EU. Even as inflation declined, households continued to face substantially higher prices, while withheld EU funds further restricted the government’s economic room for manoeuvre. Serbian households also experienced considerable inflation, although to a lesser degree. Yet economic dissatisfaction alone cannot explain the governments’ defeats. Both had survived previous elections despite mounting economic difficulties and public frustration. These conditions made the incumbents vulnerable, but why did they lose this time, rather than in earlier electoral cycles? Both governments spent years building up their influence over traditional media, particularly television, which remained an important source of political information for older and less politically engaged voters. But as online news and social media became increasingly influential, new opportunities emerged to communicate outside government-controlled channels. In Hungary, Fidesz invested heavily in online political advertising , particularly on Facebook and YouTube. However, Meta and Google stopped political advertising in the EU in 2025, restricting Fidesz’s campaigning ahead of the 2026 election. Meanwhile, Magyar built a highly successful organic social media presence. Serbia was different: outside the EU, Vucic’s party retained its online advertising advantage, but the students similarly used social media to communicate and organise independently. Neither movement relied on online campaigning alone. Both complemented their digital presence with extensive nationwide campaigns , visiting smaller towns and rural communities long dominated by the governing parties. By combining online communication with direct, face-to-face mobilisation, they reached voters who might otherwise have encountered little information beyond government-friendly media. Both opposition movements emerged from scandals that exposed the governments’ vulnerabilities. In Serbia, the collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad on November 1, 2024 killed 16 people and became a symbol of corruption and institutional failure. It triggered the student-led protests that eventually developed into a nationwide challenge to Vucic. In Hungary, the 2024 presidential pardon scandal revealed that the Fidesz-backed president had pardoned a children’s home official who helped cover up sexual abuse. The revelation undermined the government’s emphasis on child protection, forced the resignations of the president and Fidesz’s lead European Parliament candidate, and opened the way for Magyar’s political emergence. Despite their differences, both scandals made longstanding criticisms of corruption and unaccountability concrete and personal. Their significance lay not simply in the outrage they generated, but in their political consequences. Both governments had survived years of scandals and protests. What made these events different was that they helped bring about a transformation of the opposition itself. Perhaps the strongest evidence for the importance of opposition renewal comes from elections in which the new challengers were absent. In a Hungarian by-election in January 2025, Fidesz still won 64 per cent against the traditional opposition despite growing dissatisfaction. Similarly, in Serbian local elections later that year, Vucic’s governing coalition won 67 per cent against a largely traditional opposition alliance, although the vote was marred by reported irregularities. The comparison is even more striking in Hungary’s parliamentary elections. Fidesz received more than 2.1 million domestic votes in both the 2014 and 2026 elections. Yet while in 2014 this secured a two-thirds parliamentary majority for Fidesz, in 2026 it was Tisza that won such a super-majority. The decisive difference was the new opposition’s ability to unite previously fragmented voters , mobilise new supporters and attract former government voters. Economic problems, scandals and government fatigue made both governments vulnerable, but dissatisfaction alone was insufficient. It was the emergence of credible new opposition movements that turned dissatisfaction into electoral defeat. None of this means that opposition renewal alone would have been sufficient. Economic difficulties, scandals and government fatigue created the conditions for change, and without these crises, the new opposition movements might never have emerged. But it was their ability to turn widespread dissatisfaction into a credible political alternative that ultimately made the difference. The experiences of Hungary and Serbia demonstrate that even governments with extensive control over the media, state resources and political institutions are not invincible, as long as elections remain at least partly competitive. Orban and Vucic did not lose simply because voters had grown tired of them. They lost because, for the first time in years, enough voters believed there was someone capable of replacing them. Dániel Róna is a political scientist and director of the 21 Research Center. Fábián Spasic is an analyst at the 21 Research Center. The 21 Research Center is an independent Budapest-based research institute, specialising in public opinion polling, social research and political analysis. articles.title: Serbian Media Owner, Key Ally of Outgoing Administration, Arrested
articles.summary: Vucic himself confirmed the arrest in parliament, adding: “He was arrested only because of his journalistic work
articles.body: Dragan J Vucicevic, owner of the populist Serbian TV station Informer and a staunch supporter of the now-ousted administration of Aleksandar Vucic, was arrested on Wednesday on suspicion of “causing panic and disorder” and obstruction of justice. He was detained on the orders of the Second Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office in Belgrade according to Nova.rs, which said he will be placed in police custody for up to 48 hours. Vucic himself confirmed the arrest in parliament, adding: “He was arrested only because of his journalistic work.” According to the media outlet N1, Vucicevic will be brought before a prosecutor for questioning on Thursday. MPs from the Student List, which won recent elections in Serbia. applauded after Vucic’s confirmation of the arrest. After that, MPs from Vucic’s now opposition Serbian Progressive Party, SNS, left the parliamentary session for the police station where Vucicevic was being held. According to N1, that included the MPs Ana Brnabic and Milos Vucevic and a former State Secretary at the Interior Ministry, Dijana Hrkalovic. Vucicevic has been in the public spotlight since the Council of Serbia’s Regulatory Authority for Electronic Media, REM, launched two investigations into Informer. On November 16, the REM imposed two broadcasting bans on Informer, lasting 15 and 10 days respectively, as well as a seven-day ban on advertising between 6 p.m. and 9 p.m. At the time of publication, BIRN had no further details about the circumstances of Vucicevic’s arrest. BIRN asked the Ministry of Interior and the Second Basic Public Prosecutor’s Office for details, but neither replied.

articles.title: Women in the Foundation of BiH Statehood – Participated in Its Reconstruction, Yet Remained in the Shadow of Political Power
articles.summary: Two years later, at the Third Session, ten women participated, but none received a ministerial portfolio in the first Government of BiH
articles.body: Among 247 delegates at the First Session of ZAVNOBiH in 1943, only four were women, even though thousands participated in the anti-fascist struggle, organized resistance, and created conditions for renewing Bosnia and Herzegovina’s statehood. Two years later, at the Third Session, ten women participated, but none received a ministerial portfolio in the first Government of BiH. According to Fena interviewees, this disparity between their contribution to historical processes and their actual participation in political decision-making also marked women’s later position, whose role in creating the modern Bosnian and Herzegovinian state remains insufficiently recognized to this day. Marking November 25, the Statehood Day of BiH, is an opportunity to recall the decision of the First Session of the State Anti-Fascist Council for the National Liberation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, held on November 25 and 26, 1943, in Mrkonjić Grad, and the people who made those decisions possible. Among them were women whose contribution was not limited to armed combat. They worked as nurses, couriers, organizers of aid for the population, and participated in the work of national liberation committees and political organizing, often in extremely difficult wartime circumstances. Historian Aida Ličina-Ramić, a senior research associate at the Institute for History of the University of Sarajevo, emphasized that this broader engagement of women was an important part of the social and political movement within which Bosnian and Herzegovinian statehood was renewed. “When we talk about ZAVNOBiH, we often recall their sessions, the decisions adopted, and prominent political individuals, while little attention is devoted to a broader context of the National Liberation Struggle, within which the conditions for the renewal of Bosnian and Herzegovinian statehood were created. And women precisely were an important part of that movement,” Ličina-Ramić told Fena. She emphasized that women, in addition to direct combat activities, participated in organizing healthcare, caring for the wounded and children, supplying partisan units and working in local bodies of authority. For many, such an engagement represented a first serious exit from traditionally set social roles and an opportunity to participate in public and political life. Researcher and member of the Association for Culture and Art CRVENA Anderja Dugandžić, one of the authors of the digital Archive of the Anti-Fascist Struggle of Women of BiH and Yugoslavia, warned that women were a key part of the movement that enabled the session in Mrkonjić-Grad, but that later historical accounts largely focused on political decisions and male names. “They were not sidelined by accident: the story is almost always reduced to political decisions and male names, although in the National Liberation Struggle, women were fighters, underground operatives, couriers, nurses, rear-area organizers and political activists,” Dugandžić emphasized. Among participants of the First Session of ZAVNOBiH were Rada Vranješević, Mevla Jakupović, Zora Nikolić, and Danica Perović. A total of 247 delegates attended the founding assembly, and 173 councilors of ZAVNOBiH were elected at the session. Rada Vranješević, a member of the Women’s Anti-Fascist Front (AFŽ), addressed the participants of the session on behalf of the women of Bosanska Krajina. She was killed in 1944, following the German airborne raid on Drvar, and after the war was proclaimed a People’s Hero. Mevla Jakupović, a worker from Tuzla, was active in organizing the AFŽ and was one of the rare women who participated in all three sessions of ZAVNOBiH. Zora Nikolić worked in a communist and an anti-fascist movement. After the war, she was a member of parliament in the Assembly of the People’s Republic of BiH. Danica Perović was a physician who, during the war, worked in partisan units and hospitals. Dugandžić emphasized that their biographies are important testimonies to different forms of women’s political, social, and wartime engagement. “Four women out of 247 councilors, less than two percent, reflect the society in which women did not even have the right to vote until war, in which illiteracy among women, especially in rural areas, was extremely high and in which politics was understood as a male space,” she stated. She added that the number of women at the session does not reflect the true scale of their contribution. “While four of them were at the session, out in the field thousands of women bore the burden of combat and the rear: they fought, treated the wounded, carried messages, hid the injured, fed units, and organized life in liberated territories,” Dugandžić emphasized. Professor at the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences of the University of East Sarajevo, Zlatiborka Popov-Momčinović, considers that it is particularly important to recognize the contribution of women of different national and religious backgrounds. According to her assessment, their joint participation in the anti-fascist struggle reflected ZAVNOBiH’s core idea of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a multi-ethnic community of equal peoples and citizens. “Their sacrifice and heroism were often recognized only on a symbolic level, and to a lesser extent than the contribution of men,” assessed Popov-Momčinović. Although the anti-fascist movement proclaimed the emancipation of women as one of its important values, she points out that the top political functions were mostly reserved for men. “This disparity shows how tenacious patriarchy was, and has remained. Although the communist movement clearly set equality, the emancipation of women, as one of its key values, women still had a marginal role within the highest decision-making positions,” she emphasized. One of the key roles in mobilizing and socially empowering women was played by the Women’s Anti-Fascist Front. Its First National Conference was held in December 1942 in Bosanski Petrovac. The AFŽ gathered a large number of women, from rural to city areas, enabling them to participate in organizing resistance, literacy campaigns, education, and public action. Ličina-Ramić recalls that as early as the Foča Regulations of 1942 confirmed the women’s right to vote and be elected to the national liberation committee, which represented a significant step forward compared to the pre-war period. An especially important step was taken at the Second Session of ZAVNOBiH, held in 1944 in Sanski Most, when the Declaration on the Rights of Citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina strictly proclaimed the equality of women and men in political and social life. However, the realization of these rights was much more complex in practice. “Their inclusion in political life did not automatically entail an equal participation in decision-making. Women were significantly less represented in leadership positions, and patriarchal relations and traditional views of their role were also present within the National Liberation Movement itself,” explained Ličina Ramić. Dugandžić believes that the AFŽ played a decisive role in creating conditions for realizing women’s political and social rights, but warns that its abolition in 1953 represents an important turning point in the history of their organizing. “With the abolition of the AFŽ, women lost a collective body, an organization that speaks in their name and defines their real needs,” Dugandžić told Fena. Popov-Momčinović also believes that the AFŽ, despite its great contribution to emancipation, operated within a political system that did not grant it full autonomy. In her opinion, those limitations affected women’s ability to independently set political priorities and participate more strongly in decision-making. Rights Expanded, but Political Power Did not Grow at the Same Pace. Historian Aida Ličina-Ramić emphasized that post-war changes should not be observed only through limitations, because opportunities were opened to women, which they did not have in a pre-war society. They also gained political and civil rights, significantly greater access to education and employment, and their legal position in marriage and family was also changed. But traditional household division still represented an obstacle to their full participation in public life. “It’s one thing to proclaim equality, but it is a completely different thing to achieve it in everyday life. Traditional ideas about the role of women, especially in family, did not disappear with the adoption of new laws,” emphasized Ličina Ramić. Limited representation of women in political structures is also confirmed by data from her research on the socialist period. The share of women in total membership of the Communist Party in Bosnia and Herzegovina decreased from 20.43 percent in 1946 to 15.40 percent in 1953. Although the absolute number of members was increasing, their percentage share declined. Ličina-Ramić emphasized that these data do not directly show their share in leadership positions, but point to uneven political inclusion. After the AFŽ ceased operation, the Union of Women’s Societies of Bosnia and Herzegovina was founded. It focused mainly on education, healthcare, employment, and concrete problems of women’s everyday life. According to data cited by Ličina-Ramić, 290 women’s societies with approximately 35,000 members operated in BiH in 1960. The Union raised issues such as opening nurseries, kindergartens, school cafeterias, and other services that would make it easier for women to balance employment and family obligations. However, its work took place within the existing political system, and the possibility of realizing initiatives depended on different institutions and available funds. “I wouldn’t say that equality in the socialist period was only declarative. Significant progress was recorded, and new opportunities for women’s political and social action also opened. However, their inclusion in public life was not matched by corresponding representation in structures of political power,” Ličina-Ramić emphasized. Popov-Momčinović believes that it is precisely in the gap between formally recognized rights and real political influence that patterns that persisted even after major social changes can be recognized. “Just like today, the system rested on women’s unpaid and unrecognized work and on the so-called double burden, which slowed down their participation in public life and limited their real political power,” she said. While the role of women in renewing statehood and driving social changes was significant, their representation in education and public culture of remembrance is limited even today. Historian Melisa Forić from the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences of the University of Sarajevo, who researched the representation of women in contemporary history books in BiH, warned that their contribution is often presented through short and general information. “The participation of women in the National Liberation Movement during World War II and the formation of the AFŽ in most of the textbooks is presented in the form of brief information which is accompanied by photographs of female partisans, without naming them or including parts of their biographies,” Forić told Fena. According to her research, there are also significant differences in how ZAVNOBiH is presented in the curricula applied in Bosnia and Herzegovina. In textbooks in the Bosnian language, the sessions of ZAVNOBiH and their decisions are mostly interpreted in the context of renewing Bosnian and Herzegovinian statehood. In textbooks in the Croatian language, ZAVNOBiH is, in her assessment, mentioned predominantly matter-of-factly, while in textbooks in the Serbian language greater emphasis is placed on the decisions of AVNOJ and establishing the Yugoslav state. Forić believes that anti-fascist values are not sufficiently represented in contemporary history teaching nor presented as ideas of broader social significance. However, she emphasizes that in recent years more research, publications, exhibitions, and digital archives have been carried out that contribute to a different portrayal of women’s roles. She particularly highlights the projects of the Historical Museum of Bosnia and Herzegovina “Young People and World War II,” and “Wer is Walter,” within which valuable archival materials are presented to the public. “Materials on Lepa Radić, Dragica Pravica, Vahida Maglajlić, Radojka Lakić, and other important participants of the National Liberation Movement represent excellent examples of educational content that can be used very successfully in teaching, as well as encourage independent research and interest among young people,” Forić emphasized. She believes that applying such content in education could contribute to a better understanding of the past and a fuller culture of memory. Popov-Momčinović warns that the insufficient representation of women in historical accounts is not only a matter of lack of research, but also of how the past is traditionally presented. “The focus was on political and military leaders, almost exclusively men,” she said. In her words, education and public discourse long reproduced historical narratives in which men were presented as the main drivers of political change, while women remained on their margins. As an example of neglecting the women’s anti-fascist heritage, she cites the attitude toward monuments and public memorials dedicated to participants of the National Liberation Struggle. She specifically pointed to the condition of the monument to Radojka Lakić, one of the better-known anti-fascists, assessing that its neglect shows insufficient care for preserving the memory of women’s contributions. She believes that biographies of women who took part in renewing statehood should receive a more prominent place in educational programs, museum displays, documentary films, and Statehood Day commemorations. articles.summary: Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there
articles.body: The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself. Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base. In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts. Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC . He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September. A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently. The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.” She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death. Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].” A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.” Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025. Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.” She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food. Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent. Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.

Pro-Palestine activist sought by US in extradition case: ‘I still have a right to my beliefs’
articles.body: James “Fergie” Chambers, the wealthy leftwing activist and donor controversially sought in extradition by the US, has told the Guardian that he is “not asking anyone to endorse my ideas or not think I’m a jerk – but I still have a right to my beliefs and should not be unjustly accused because of them”. Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza. The complaint also includes riot and conspiracy to riot charges stemming from 2023 protests against New England branches of Israeli weapons manufacturer Elbit. Chambers was speaking from his Madrid apartment in his first in-depth interview after a Spanish appeals court ordered his provisional release on bail on Friday . That release was due to issues with the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported by the Guardian. “Support for my case doesn’t imply support of me, or my ideas,” Chambers said. “It’s about my right to have those ideas – and not be falsely accused of things.” Chambers, whose case has gained attention across the world, had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza. The order granting Chambers’s provisional release asserted that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”. Spanish judges had previously denied bail three times. The wealthy heir to at least $250mn from his family’s business – Atlanta–based Cox Enterprises – was in the middle of his first visit without being separated by glass with his mother, Lauren Hamilton, when he was summoned to receive the “good news” on Friday, Chambers told the Guardian. Minutes later, he returned to tell his mother he was being released. “She freaked out crying. We went nuts for about five minutes. Then we got to contacting my lawyer and getting my kids on a plane to Spain.” On Monday, Chambers’s five-year-old son with actor and activist Stella Schnabel could be heard in the background. The tableau was in stark contrast to his months in prison. “I tried to build a cocoon to deal with the immense unknown, the immense fear,” he said of his time in Aranjuez prison. “I would pray a lot. The only idea I could hold onto was, my home is the truth. The truth of who loves you. The truth of my own innocence. And the truth of what is happening in Palestine and all the things connected to what is happening in Palestine – other wars, gas prices. No one can take that away from you.” Chambers has been supported by his mother throughout his case, and has reconnected with his father, James Cox Chambers – who owns an estimated 17% stake in Cox Enterprises but does not play an active role in the company – for the first time in five years. “Speaking with my parents has provided emotional stability – and intelligent, adult minds to help make decisions,” Chambers said. Although he has had political disagreements with his father, a donor to the Democratic party, Chambers said his father “sees this situation as totally unthinkable and out of step with anything resembling a just society”. He also invoked his grandfather, the ACLU civil rights lawyer James Cox Hamilton, who died in 2014. “He would’ve turned in his grave over this,” Chambers said. While locked up, Chambers, a US citizen, received hundreds of letters of support from friends, family and strangers, postmarked from Atlanta to Barcelona – including, he said, “from a guy who had been imprisoned under [Spanish dictator Francisco] Franco, who painted the ‘ key of return ’ [a symbol of homes lost in the 1948 Nakba] on the Palestinian flag”. Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.” His release followed a separate decision on Thursday by a three-judge panel at Spain’s high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish. The US admitted to making several of the changes, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent”. These and dozens of other changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian last week. It was also recently revealed that there is no indictment behind the complaint, meaning the federal government has not had a grand jury evaluate evidence against Chambers, and instead is seeking his extradition based on the affidavit of a single FBI agent, the core of the sealed criminal complaint. During his time in prison, Chambers also began the process of applying for political asylum in Spain. He cannot be extradited until the asylum case runs its course, and also cannot be extradited if he is granted asylum. His legal team has notified the government office evaluating his asylum petition of the altered translations. Chambers was arrested 10 July as he and Schnabel pulled into the driveway of a school they were visiting to see about enrolling their five-year-old, part of plans to move to Spain. They had been staying in Ireland, where Schnabel was working on a film. Although the arrest came as a surprise – “I was confused! Did I speed?” he thought – Chambers revealed to the Guardian that a car had been following him around Dublin only days before, and that someone had broken into their car parked outside their house at night, without taking anything of value. “I noticed signs of surveillance,” he said. Months later, last Wednesday, Irish police raided the same house, acting on a request from US authorities. With his immediate future uncertain, Chambers said he was “looking forward to sharing a couple of nice dinners with my family this week”. As for the past, he said the millions he has donated to an estimated 100 projects in about 20 countries is “the most important thing I’ve done”. “Somebody with the political orientation I have and with resources, no matter how good of an activist I am, it’s not gonna be as effective as medical aid or feeding children in Gaza, supporting independent media that wouldn’t otherwise exist, or paying people’s bail who have been arrested for protesting. “I’m giving a lot of money to things that other people aren’t giving money to.” Chambers also said he was “grateful for the way Spanish courts have dealt with this – just focusing on the facts. It shouldn’t matter that I’ve made some emotional statements.”

articles.summary: Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Tuesday that Iran is developing chemical weapons, and vowed to stop Tehran from obtaining them
articles.body:
Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Tuesday that Iran is developing chemical weapons, and vowed to stop Tehran from obtaining them.

"Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons," Katz said in a briefing to Israeli reporters, according to public broadcaster KAN and other national outlets. "The state of Israel will not allow them to reach that capability."

In his briefing on Tuesday, Katz floated the possibility of a preemptive strike against Tehran, if necessary.

"If we recognize that the Iranians intend to attack Israel, can't we tell the army to attack earlier and thwart the threat?" he said, according to a transcript from Israel's Channel 12. "If the Iranians attack us first, it will be a failure."

Katz's comments came at the same time as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi criticized the U.S. government for not funding the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, the international body that monitors and combats chemical weapons use at The Hague. The organization is facing a budget crisis because the U.S. has pulled funding, according to a Reuters report.

"The U.S. is so concerned about chemical arms that it's crippling the world's chemical weapons watchdog," Araghchi wrote Tuesday on X. "OPCW may be forced to suspend work and scale back vital programs. By obstructing its mandate, the U.S. is deliberately putting global peace and security at risk. Shameful."

The OPCW won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013 for its work in Syria.

articles.title: COVER STORY Why spy agency chief nominee is under scrutiny
articles.summary: Critics, however, cite her lack of intelligence experience and her alleged closeness to China
articles.body: Former Justice Minister Kang Kum-sil, nominated to head the National Intelligence Service, leaves her home in Seoul, Tuesday, a day after President Lee Jae Myung nominated her. Yonhap President Lee Jae Myung’s nomination of former Justice Minister Kang Kum-sil as chief of the nation's top spy agency is drawing mixed reactions over whether she is fit for the position. Supporters say Kang is an apolitical pick with experience in leading a government organization and is suitable for a time of strained ties with Washington. Critics, however, cite her lack of intelligence experience and her alleged closeness to China. If confirmed by the National Assembly, Kang, 69, would lead the National Intelligence Service (NIS), an agency central to national security, at a time when Seoul’s ties with Washington are strained over several issues, including Coupang and intelligence sharing. The U.S. has been limiting intelligence sharing with Seoul, a move that is believed to stem from Washington’s suspicion that Unification Minister Chung Dong-young publicly disclosed intelligence on North Korea that Washington had shared with Seoul. Talks between the allies on building nuclear-powered vessels and on Korea’s investment plans in the U.S. have also stalled. 'Blank canvas' Some experts described Kang, who has stayed out of mainstream politics for over a decade, as a "blank slate" who could put Korea’s national interests ahead of the political considerations that have strained ties with Washington. Park Chang-hwan, a professor at Jangan University, said the nomination carries a sense of change, comparing it with Kang’s earlier tenure as the first female justice minister. “There was a feeling that she would bring change to the top-down culture of a male-dominated, seniority-driven institution. This is an unconventional, new approach to choosing an NIS chief,” he said. He said replacing the faction of top officials who seek self-reliance and less influence from the U.S., is meaningful in itself. Chung and the outgoing NIS chief Lee Jong-seok have usually been categorized as part of this faction. “She’s like a blank canvas — you can paint anything on it. That could clear away the preconceptions her counterparts have about whom they’re dealing with. For the intelligence organization to be able to support diplomacy centered on the national interest that President Lee wants, she’s not a bad choice.” Park, however, questioned Kang’s ability to lead the agency. “She also has no experience in intel, and an intelligence agency does work behind the scenes that directly affects the national interest.” Shin Yul, a political science professor at Myongji University, said Kang's distance from partisan thinking makes her a better choice for handling tensions with Washington. “If the choice is between someone with defense and security expertise and someone who lacks that expertise but isn’t constrained by partisan thinking, I think the latter is the better choice right now,” Shin said. Kang Kum-sil, special presidential envoy and ambassador for global climate and environment, speaks at the Antalya Leaders Summit of the 31st Conference of the Parties to the U.N. Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31) in Antalya, Turkey, Nov. 12. Courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs Alleged China ties Kang’s critics point to her past roles in China. She previously served as a special adviser to the Qiqihar Municipal People’s Government in northeastern China's Heilongjiang province in 2013 and as a special economic adviser to the Yanbian Korean Autonomous Prefecture in 2014. Political commentator Jang Seong-cheol said her ties to China could make it harder to mend relations with Washington. “Kang has appeared quite close to China and she previously opposed the U.S.-backed deployment of THAAD. How will Washington take this nomination?” Jang said in an MBC show. Jang also suggested the nomination was a reward for political support. “She has never worked in intelligence," he said. "She twice chaired President Lee’s fundraising committee and served as his overall campaign chair in the latest election. That makes me wonder whether the nomination is a reward for her support. I don’t think she was the right choice.” Opposition party lawmakers also criticized the nomination, claiming Kang lacks intelligence experience and is biased toward China, and urged Lee to withdraw it. Rep. Ahn Cheol-soo of the main opposition People Power Party (PPP) described Kang as pro-China and warned “Kang will cause the Korea-U.S. alliance to collapse.” “She hasn't simply been supportive of China. She has taken an active role by working for China in an official capacity and praising its leader ... President Lee must withdraw the nomination immediately,” Ahn said on Facebook. PPP spokesperson Rep. Park Choong-kwon said the presidential office had “put someone with no intelligence experience at the heart of the country’s intelligence apparatus.” “A single misjudgment by an intelligence agency can quickly lead to a national security disaster,” Park said, adding that the PPP would closely scrutinize Kang’s qualifications at her confirmation hearing. Professor Shin, however, rejected the pro-China label. “People point to things Kang did in China, but I don’t think that’s enough to call her pro-China,” he said.

articles.title: AfD co-leader says no peace in Europe without working with US, Russia
articles.summary: BERLIN, November 25
articles.body: BERLIN, November 25. /TASS/. Peace in Europe can only be reached together with Russia and the United States, and the coalition of the willing on Ukraine only hinders efforts to resolve the conflict, Alice Weidel, a co-chairwoman of the Alternative for Germany (AfD) opposition party, argued. "Your 'coalition of the willing' is actually a coalition of the helpless," the politician said during debates on the 2027 draft budget at the Bundestag, addressing German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. "It does not contribute to putting an end to the Ukraine conflict, but stands in the way of peace. Remember one thing: peace in Europe is only possible jointly with Russia and the United States, not without them," she stressed. Weidel pointed out that Germany spends €18 billion annually on Ukraine, including the costs of accommodating refugees from this country in Germany and €11.5 billion as military aid to Kiev. Alongside her AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla, Weidel called Ukraine "one of the most corrupt countries," noting that Germany will soon be the only nation to finance Kiev. articles.title: Number of women killed by men in Ireland almost doubles in a year
articles.summary: That should alarm every one of us,” said Sarah Benson, the organisation’s chief executive
articles.body: The number of women in Ireland killed by men has surged in the past five years and risen especially sharply in the past 12 months, according to a study. After falling for two decades, the number of violent deaths began going up in 2021 and has risen sharply this year, with 13 deaths so far, the report by Irish charity Women’s Aid said on Wednesday. “That should alarm every one of us,” said Sarah Benson, the organisation’s chief executive. “After years of decline, the number of women killed is rising again.” The vast majority of victims over the past three decades were killed by a man they knew and over half were killed by a current or former partner. The findings match UN and EU data showing the most dangerous place for a woman is her own home, and the most likely killer is a man she knows, said Benson. “Ireland is one of the wealthiest countries in the world, and we have good laws. Yet women are still being killed by the men closest to them. Most men choose never to behave this way, and that is exactly why we need everyone to recognise this violence and call it out.” Since 1996, when the Dublin-based charity began collating femicide statistics, 291 women have been killed by men. Measured in five-year blocks, the levels of violent deaths peaked at 67 between 1996 and 2000 and fell to a low of 31 between 2016 and 2020. During the 2021–2025 period, 40 deaths were recorded, a 29% increase on the previous period. The 13 women who died in violent circumstances this year is almost double the figure of seven for all of last year. However, Ireland’s overall murder rate of 0.66 per 100,000 people remains well below global and European averages. The country has a population of 5.5 million. Of the 235 cases of violent deaths resolved since 1996, 89% of the women were killed by a man known to them, 57% were killed by a current or former partner, 32% by a male relative or acquaintance and 11% by a male stranger. More than two-thirds – 68% – died in their own homes. Just over a quarter were women aged 26 to 35. “Intimate partner femicide rarely comes out of nowhere,” said Benson. “Separation, coercive control, non-fatal strangulation, threats to kill and stalking are all known warning signs. When a woman tells Women’s Aid that she is afraid for her life, we believe her.” Leaving an abusive partner did not always end abuse, said Benson. “Risk rises sharply around separation and stays high for about a year. For every woman whose life is taken, thousands more are living on a knife’s edge of fear.” The Femicide Watch report, which coincided with International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, recorded that 25 children were killed alongside a woman, usually their mother.

articles.title: Iran criticizes U.S. for using artificial intelligence for deadly attacks
articles.summary: Iran has denounced the US military's use of artificial intelligence to plan and carry out attacks
articles.body:
Iran has denounced the U.S. military's use of artificial intelligence to plan and carry out attacks.

Speaking at a U.N. Security Council meeting Tuesday, Iranian Ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi said the weaponization of AI "raises serious concerns."

Darzi claimed U.S. forces used the technology to deploy more than 2,000 munitions to hit 2,000 distinct targets within 96 hours. He said Palantir's Maven and Anthropic's Claude system were used to analyze intelligence, identify and prioritize targets and provide strike coordinates.

"Neither advanced technology nor the involvement of private companies can shield the United States or the Israeli regime from accountability for flagrant violations of their obligations under international law," Darzi told the council meeting.

"Those responsible for the commission of atrocious crimes against Iranian people, including deliberate attacks against civilians and civilian objects, must face individual criminal accountability," he added.

In March 2026, the Commander of U.S. Central Command Adm. Brad Cooper confirmed American forces had used a "variety of advanced AI tools" in order to "cut through the noise and make smarter decisions faster than the enemy can react."

While the Pentagon has not said exactly how AI tools are being deployed, CBS News spoke in March with several experts with knowledge of military operations who described the likely scenarios.

"The military is now processing roughly a thousand potential targets a day and striking the majority of them, with turnaround time for the next strike potentially under four hours," said retired Navy Admiral Mark Montgomery, senior director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracy's Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation. "A human is still in the loop, but AI is doing the work that used to take days of analysis — and doing it at a scale no previous campaign has matched."
