editorialRejections.title: Defence Minister Denies Albanian Involvement in Attack on Russian Vessel
editorialRejections.summary: No evidence that Iranian opposition activities in Albania triggered Iran’s 2022 cyberattack, Nufi says
editorialRejections.reason: Russia coverage requires an international or Russian news source
editorialRejections.body: No evidence that Iranian opposition activities in Albania triggered Iran’s 2022 cyberattack, Nufi says. TIRANA, Albania – Albania’s Defence Minister Ermal Nufi has rejected allegations linking Albanian territory to a recent attack on a Russian vessel off the Libyan coast, while dismissing claims that the activities of Iranian opposition members sheltered in Albania triggered Tehran’s massive cyberattack against the country in 2022. Speaking to ABC News on Tuesday evening, Nufi addressed two separate security issues that illustrate Albania’s exposure to international geopolitical conflicts, hybrid threats and disinformation campaigns. The minister categorically denied that Albanian territory had been used to launch the attack against a Russian vessel near Benghazi, Libya, on November 21. Allegations of Albanian involvement, initially circulated by several Turkish online media outlets, were described by Nufi as part of a deliberate disinformation campaign. Nufi said Ukraine had claimed responsibility for the operation, which involved maritime drone technology that the Albanian Armed Forces do not possess. He also stressed that Albania, as a NATO member, would not undertake a military operation of this nature without coordination with the Alliance. The incident nevertheless highlights the risks associated with the geographical expansion of the Russian-Ukrainian conflict beyond the immediate theatre of war. For Albania, attempts to associate its territory with military operations against Russia represent a potentially serious security challenge, even when such allegations are unsubstantiated. Addressing relations with Iran, Nufi said there was no evidence that the activities of the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK), whose members are accommodated in Manza, near Durrës, had triggered the Iranian cyberattack against Albania in 2022. According to the minister, investigations and inspections conducted by Albanian authorities had found no evidence linking the activities of the camp’s residents to Tehran’s attack. He noted that their average age was over 60 and that the organization operated internationally, with its principal centre in France. Nufi reiterated the humanitarian nature of Albania’s decision to accommodate the Iranian opposition members. The initial request dated back to 2012, while the arrangement was formalized in 2016, following deadly attacks against members of the organization in Iraq. The Iranian cyberattack in 2022, which prompted Albania to sever diplomatic relations with Tehran, marked a turning point in the country’s national security environment, demonstrating its vulnerability to unconventional forms of foreign aggression. Nufi also warned that the escalation of the war in Ukraine and recent tensions along the Estonian-Russian border posed serious threats to regional and international security. He reaffirmed NATO’s defensive mission and highlighted the growing importance of addressing hybrid threats and cyberattacks. Although the Iranian cyberattack and the allegations surrounding the Russian vessel are fundamentally different, both illustrate how Albania’s security is increasingly affected by conflicts and geopolitical rivalries extending far beyond the Western Balkans. For a small NATO member with limited national defence capabilities, cybersecurity, intelligence cooperation, institutional resilience and the ability to counter disinformation are becoming increasingly important components of national security. The principal challenge for Albania is to maintain its international commitments and strategic alignment with NATO while preventing its territory from becoming, or being portrayed as, a platform for military confrontation with third countries.

editorialRejections.title: Defense minister in parliament: Ukraine not using Estonian airspace to attack Russia
editorialRejections.summary: Herem explained that Ukrainian drones have entered Estonian airspace because of technical issues or as a result of Russian electronic countermeasures
editorialRejections.reason: Ukraine coverage requires an international news source
editorialRejections.body: Defense Minister Martin Herem said in Riigikogu that Ukrainian drones are not using Estonian airspace to attack Russia and that Ukraine has never asked Estonia for permission to do so. Herem explained that Ukrainian drones have entered Estonian airspace because of technical issues or as a result of Russian electronic countermeasures. Unaffiliated MP Varro Vooglaid stated as fact that Ukrainians are using Estonian airspace for drone attacks against Russia and expressed the view that Russia could eventually respond forcefully. "If one state allows its airspace or other territory to be used to attack another state, thereby enabling such attacks, it is regarded as a participant in that military attack," Vooglaid said. "What has the government actually done, or what does it intend to do, to draw a line against the use of our airspace for carrying out such attacks?" Vooglaid asked. Herem replied that Estonia has not made its airspace available to Ukraine. "Moreover, Ukraine has never asked for it. Secondly, we have told Ukraine to avoid using our airspace," Herem said. "You are presenting your hypothesis as a fact. You claim that we have granted access — we have not. Out of the hundreds and thousands of drones Ukraine launches against targets in Russia, only a few have strayed into our airspace or that of our allies. That in no way proves that we permit it. Otherwise, considering the number of drones and the time they spend in the air, one would also have to accuse Russia of allowing it all to happen, because far more of them fly there for much longer periods. As for sensors and air defense systems, Russia does not always detect them and cannot shoot all of them down either. Therefore, the occasional overflight cannot be used to claim that we have made our airspace available," Herem said. Vooglaid then said that he had never claimed Estonia had authorized the use of its airspace for Ukrainian military attacks. "I never claimed that we had authorized it. You attributed that claim to me yourself. The question is not whether we granted permission or not, although I also suspect that perhaps permission has been given, but I cannot claim that because I do not have such information. The fact remains that our airspace is being used to carry out these attacks. There can be no dispute about that. This was not a one-time incident, nor a second or third incident. It has happened many times already. I don't even know how many times anymore. Our airspace has repeatedly been used for carrying out these attacks," Vooglaid said. Vooglaid asked again whether telling Ukraine not to use Estonian airspace was the only thing the government had done to stop "the use of Estonian airspace for this kind of warfare." "They shrug their shoulders and use it again and again and again. What happens next? Do you simply tell them once more that they may not use our airspace for warfare, or are there additional measures? Some actual expression of protest, summoning the Ukrainian ambassador, issuing an ultimatum, or military measures to prevent Ukrainian war drones from flying through our airspace?" "And if you say the problem is limited sensor and air defense capabilities, then I would ask why we are investing money in national defense at all if we cannot stop drones. If drones were to come from Russia toward Estonia, would our capability then be any greater, or just as inadequate as it is now?" Vooglaid added. In his response, Herem again stated that Ukraine is not using Estonian airspace. "These drones enter our airspace for technical reasons, human reasons, countermeasure-related reasons or weather-related reasons. That does not mean anyone is deliberately using it. How do we know that? We simply observe the trajectories of these aircraft. They fly mainly through Russian airspace, while only a few enter ours," Herem said. "If you say Ukrainians are using it and we are doing nothing about it, then once again look at what is happening in Russia. Many more drones fly there unhindered and without being stopped. We cannot somehow blame ourselves for the fact that these aircraft occasionally end up here. We have discussed this with the Ukrainians. They maintain that the few drones that enter our airspace out of thousands do so unintentionally," Herem said. "Why do we invest in defense at all? To be better prepared against threats like these. If we knew such investments would have absolutely no effect should drones start coming from Russia, then there truly would be no point in making them," Herem added. MP Varro Vooglaid has repeatedly argued on social media that Ukraine uses Estonian airspace for drone attacks against targets in Russia and that Estonia has enabled Ukraine to do so.

editorialRejections.title: Leaked data shows 490,000 Russian forces have died in Ukraine war Russian government data obtained by pro-Ukraine hackers and analyzed by the BBC indicates that Russia has lost at least 490,334 soldiers during its war on Ukraine. 6h ago

editorialRejections.body: More than 490,000 Russian soldiers have died since Vladimir Putin ordered Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, according to leaked Russian government data analyzed by CBS News partner network BBC News. Another organization's analysis of the vast dataset suggests the toll is likely closer to 700,000.A recent hack by pro-Ukraine groups Belarusian Cyber Partisans BY and Ukraine's Silent Crow produced the data that was analyzed by the BBC and independent Russian outlet Mediazona. It included more than 11 million death records from 2021 to September 2026, according to the British broadcaster.The data, which includes granular information on the location of deaths in Ukraine and Russian border regions, age ranges, causes of death, and employment and court rulings suggests at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have died during the war so far, according to the BBC. According to Mediazona's analysis, which the outlet said accounted for delays in death registrations, missing records and deaths occurring since the data was leaked, Russia's total military death toll has likely reached around 700,000. In May, the head of the United Kingdom's communications and cyber spy agency also put the number of Russian military deaths during the war at about 500,000, citing Western intelligence."Putin is going backwards on the battlefield, with new intelligence showing that almost half a million Russian soldiers have been killed since the conflict began," Anne Keast-Butler, the director of the Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ), said at the time.The Kremlin has not publicly revealed the Russian death toll from the war. Ukrainian President Zelenskyy said for the first time in February that his country's losses stood at 55,000. That figure has not been independently corroborated, however, and the Center for Strategic and International Studies think tank estimated as many as 150,000 Ukrainian fatalities up to June 2026.The BBC also reported that the leaked data shows 65% of 18- to 24-year-olds in Russia who died in 2025 were casualties of the war. For Russians aged 25-34 last year, the number was 59%, making the war the main cause of death for young Russian adults last year, according to the data.When asked about the various reports surfacing from the data leak, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Wednesday: "The only entity that can officially disclose casualty figures is the Defense Ministry of the Russian Federation.""I suggest not to pay attention to any other data," he said.

editorialRejections.reason: US coverage requires an international or US news source
editorialRejections.body: The US Army has officially fielded its first Long Range Hypersonic Weapon battery, according to the service’s top general in charge of munitions, Breaking defense reports. “It is fully fielded. It is ready to go,” Lt. Gen. Frank Lozano, Program Acquisition Executive (PAE) for Fires, told Breaking Defense on Nov. 19 during an interview. “It is a global deployable and employable warfighting capability. Those soldiers and those units have everything that they need to employ, fight and win.” Lozano declined to disclose when or where the first battery was fielded, offering few details about the milestone beyond confirming that the weapon is operational and ready for deployment. The news comes after years of challenges with developing and fielding the LHRW, also known as the Dark Eagle. The Army initially planned to field the first battery in 2023, but testing woes — including a mechanical engineering problem with the launcher — prevented the service from meeting that goal. The Army later pushed its fielding target to September 2025, but missed that deadline as well. According to a recent report from Bloomberg, the Army had still not completely fielded its first LRHW battery as of October 2026 — putting the service nearly three years behind schedule. The Army’s program office reportedly said in a statement to Bloomberg at the time that it “continues fielding activities” for the Dark Eagle and must undergo more training and other sustainment and readiness work “before declaring the system fully fielded.” When asked if the report from October were inaccurate, Lozano said he didn’t “want to go so far as to say that.” Instead, he said “this is a rapidly evolving space, and things can happen very quickly, and for all the right reasons, we in the Army and we at PAE [Program Acquisition Executive] Fires are being very, very aggressive about producing, developing and fielding new capabilities that include Dark Eagle.” Asked when the first battery officially reached full fielding status, Lozano pointed to the fact that some of the weapon’s ground support equipment had been delivered as early as 2021, making it difficult to identify a specific date for the milestone.

editorialRejections.title: Why Indian nationals are still ending up in Russia's war on Ukraine
editorialRejections.summary: But instead of finding work as a driver, he was sent to fight in Ukraine for the Russian armed forces
editorialRejections.reason: Why headlines are excluded
editorialRejections.body: Gurpreet Singh Randhawa, a 40-year-old from Jalandhar in India's northern Punjab state, said he traveled to Russia for work after responding to a Facebook advertisement for a driving job at a garment factory. But instead of finding work as a driver, he was sent to fight in Ukraine for the Russian armed forces . After escaping from his unit, he surrendered to Ukrainian forces in November. He is now being held as a prisoner of war. In an interview with Ukrainian YouTuber Volodymyr Zolkin, Randhawa described how, after arriving in Russia, he was taken to a military facility, made to sign a contract and sent for training. He said they confiscated his passport and phone. His account has not been independently verified. He is the second Indian national known to have escaped the Russian military. Sahil Majothi, a 23-year-old from Gujarat, surrendered to Ukrainian forces in October 2025. He had joined the Russian military while serving a prison sentence in Russia, reportedly believing that military service would help him secure his release. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The cases underline how little has changed since Prime Minister Narendra Modi raised the issue with Russian President Vladimir Putin during his visit to Moscow in July 2024 . At the time, Putin assured him that Indians who were misled into joining the Russian army would be discharged. But the recruitment of Indians has continued. In an October filing before the Supreme Court, India's Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) said approximately 267 Indians have joined the Russian armed forces since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine . Of these, 139 were discharged and 51 were killed. The whereabouts of the 77 others were unknown. Russian authorities have confirmed that seven of them are missing. The problem extends beyond Indians who travel to Russia seeking civilian employment, only to find themselves exposed to recruitment networks and the dangers of a war zone. The MEA has also highlighted cases of Indians knowingly enlisting in the Russian military for the supposed financial benefits on offer, believing they could later secure release through government intervention. Some had also approached Indian authorities to renounce their citizenship and obtain Russian passports. "This is a dangerous path and is strongly discouraged by the government," the ministry said. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Former diplomat Anil Trigunayat said the growing movement of Indian workers to Russia presents both economic opportunities and new challenges for their protection. "Inadequate oversight of recruitment networks could leave vulnerable workers exposed to exploitation," Trigunayat told DW. He said Indian workers were often burdened by substantial recruitment fees and continued deductions from their salaries by intermediaries. "Some of them had paid between 300,000 to 500,000 Indian rupees [$5,400 /€4,900] to Indian recruitment agents, and even while working in Russia, more than 30% of their agreed monthly salary was taken away by local and foreign agents," Trigunayat said. The former diplomat added that some Indians who had overstayed their visas in Russia were particularly vulnerable. Military service was allegedly offered to earn substantial wages and regularize their immigration status. Mohammad Sufiyan, from Hyderabad in the southern state of Telangana, said he was lured to Russia under false pretences and forced into active combat in Ukraine. He had traveled abroad in search of employment and a better livelihood, but ended up in a war zone. He has since returned home to India . "Many people are duped. Some decide it is better to seek citizenship than come back to India. It's a tough life, and people will go to any lengths to get some sort of employment," Sufiyan told DW. Sufiyan's experience points to the economic desperation that makes such offers attractive, even when they carry the risk of being caught up in a war. Rajan Kumar, a professor at the Center for Russian and Central Asian Studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University's School of International Studies, said some Indians who traveled to Russia for work could find themselves caught up in the fighting without having joined the military. "Some of them, they don't join the army, but they end up in the army region. They're caught in the crossfire," Kumar told DW. He said India was negotiating with Moscow to secure the return of its citizens caught up in such situations. "Russia is very cooperative so far," he said. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video India has been pressing Russia to take action, but the issue persists. The recruitment efforts reflect Russia's need for more manpower for its nearly five-year war in Ukraine , and the limited influence New Delhi can exert over Moscow, despite the close political relationship between the two countries. Mohsin Raza Khan, a professor at the Jindal School of International Affairs, told DW that Putin 's need to sustain the war effort was taking precedence over the concerns of a strategic partner. He points out that the Russian president was reluctant to impose another mobilization on his own population for fear of domestic unrest. "In these circumstances, sustaining the war effort appears to take precedence over concerns raised by India. Neither Modi nor New Delhi has sufficient leverage to change that," said Khan. Khan also said the willingness of some Indians to enlist, and even consider giving up their citizenship, is down to the lack of decent employment opportunities at home. "For young, educated men without contacts or connections, the chances of respectable employment are so low that the risks of a high casualty war are preferable," he said.

editorialRejections.title: Two Newly Disclosed GeoServer Vulnerabilities Under Attack
editorialRejections.summary: Attackers are probing GeoServer instances for two high-severity flaws that can be chained with other bugs for unauthenticated RCE
editorialRejections.reason: No DNU heading could be identified
editorialRejections.body: Attackers are probing GeoServer instances for two high-severity flaws that can be chained with other bugs for unauthenticated RCE. Threat actors are targeting two recently disclosed GeoServer vulnerabilities that can be chained with other flaws to achieve unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). Cybersecurity firm WatchTowr has observed attempts to exploit two high-severity GeoServer vulnerabilities tracked as CVE-2026-120705 and CVE-2026-129243. The activity appears to be aimed at identifying vulnerable servers. “Attackers sent error-based exploit probes to validate that the server is vulnerable by creating and invoking stored queries,” WatchTowr noted. WatchTowr has not reported any instances of attackers successfully achieving remote code execution. At the time of writing there do not appear to be any other reports of exploitation attempts. GeoServer is an open source application for publishing and sharing geospatial data. Government agencies widely use it, and utilities also deploy it. Cybersecurity company Eye Security has identified more than 3,000 internet-accessible GeoServer instances. CVE-2026-120705 is an XML injection vulnerability that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to obtain sensitive files or conduct server-side request forgery (SSRF) attacks. CVE-2026-129243 can enable attackers to bypass access controls and perform operations typically reserved for administrators. The two security holes are part of a five-bug exploit chain discovered by Rapid7 researcher Jonah Burgess, aka CryptoCat, who reported his findings to GeoServer developers in early August. Burgess also reported CVE-2026-129244, CVE-2026-129245, and CVE-2026-129242. He showed how an attacker can gain admin access and execute arbitrary commands with the GeoServer process’s privileges. The researcher disclosed technical details this week and published PoC exploit code. Eye Security has independently found some of the vulnerabilities. It demonstrated unauthenticated RCE on Linux and Windows by combining three weaknesses: CVE-2026-120705, CVE-2026-129245, and CVE-2026-120704. The security firm said it reported its findings to the vendor in late September. GeoServer released patches several weeks ago, and it published advisories in recent days. Organizations are advised to upgrade to GeoServer 3.0.2, 2.28.6, or 2.27.7. GeoServer vulnerabilities have been targeted in the past. In August 2026, hackers exploited a vulnerability as a zero-day, and in 2025 it came to light that a US government agency had been breached through the exploitation of a GeoServer flaw. editorialRejections.title: Suspected ransomware attack disrupts cancer treatments, surgeries at Guadeloupe hospital
editorialRejections.summary: French prosecutors have launched a criminal investigation into the incident
editorialRejections.reason: No DNU heading could be identified
editorialRejections.body: France’s national cybersecurity agency is investigating a suspected ransomware attack that impaired the computer systems of the University Hospital of Guadeloupe, forcing doctors to postpone surgeries, suspend some cancer treatments and revert to pen and paper. France’s national cybersecurity agency, known as ANSSI, said Tuesday the incident appeared to involve ransomware and that investigators were examining whether hackers gained access to the hospital’s systems through an unnamed IT supplier that was reportedly compromised several months ago. French prosecutors have launched a criminal investigation into the incident. It remains unclear who was behind the attack. The hospital’s management told local media on Monday that it had not received a ransom demand and ruled out paying a ransom. The hospital — the largest on the French Caribbean island of approximately 380,000 residents — said on its website it had canceled some surgical procedures, medical consultations and imaging tests through at least Friday. Radiation therapy has been temporarily suspended over safety concerns, while chemotherapy sessions scheduled for Monday were canceled. The hospital is reviewing upcoming appointments based on each patient’s medical needs. Emergency services, dialysis treatments and urgent cardiac procedures remain available. The hospital has asked residents to visit its emergency departments only if they need immediate medical care. Hospital employees first experienced computer and telephone outages on Saturday evening, according to local media reports. What initially appeared to be a technical malfunction turned out to be a cyberattack that encrypted the hospital’s databases. “We’re back to pen and paper, relying on couriers who travel from one department to another,” the hospital’s director told local media. As of Tuesday, healthcare workers were still unable to access patients’ electronic medical records and were manually processing prescriptions and collecting laboratory results, slowing patient care. The hospital has encouraged patients to bring paper copies of their medical records, prescriptions and previous test results to appointments. It remains unclear whether the hackers stole any personal or medical information. The hospital said it would notify anyone whose data was compromised and warned patients to watch out for phishing attempts by criminals posing as hospital staff. The hospital plans to gradually restore the affected systems after checking them for malware. Recovery is expected to take several days, but it remains unclear when normal operations will fully resume. The attack came as the hospital was relocating its operations to a new facility in Belle-Plaine. The French government financed the construction of the new hospital after a major fire damaged its previous facilities in 2017. According to hospital management, the new facility’s computer systems have stronger security protections, making the disruption easier to manage there. Despite the attack, the hospital has maintained its plans to transfer pediatric emergency services to the new site. Two other French healthcare organizations — Bordeaux University Hospital and France’s National Cancer Institute — disclosed cyberattacks earlier this week. Bordeaux University Hospital said it discovered its computer systems had been compromised after detecting that two of its email accounts had been used to send mass emails to employees. A threat actor known as Scarlettgroup claimed responsibility for the breach, threatening to publish allegedly stolen medical records, prescriptions, laboratory results and financial documents. The hospital has not confirmed the hackers’ claims and is investigating whether any information was stolen. It temporarily restricted external access to one of its servers as a precaution but said the incident had not disrupted patient care. France’s National Cancer Institute confirmed Monday that a cyberattack had compromised personal information and disrupted two of its websites. The institute said it had stopped the intrusion but has not disclosed how many people were affected or what information was exposed. French Health Minister Stephanie Rist said Tuesday the government was working to improve cybersecurity across the country’s healthcare sector and planned to secure long-term funding for these efforts through France’s proposed 2027 social security budget. “The cybersecurity of our hospitals is also the safety of our patients,” Rist added. is a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

editorialRejections.title: 'Sputnik S' Vs. Starlink: What Happens When A Nuclear Weapon Explodes In Space?
editorialRejections.summary: That claim was swiftly denied by the Kremlin amid increasing unease over the militarization of space
editorialRejections.reason: Question headlines are excluded
editorialRejections.body: Reports emerged on November 23 that Russia is planning the launch of a nuclear-armed satellite, named Sputnik-S into space “at any time in the coming weeks" after years of storing the alleged weapon in the Moscow region. That claim was swiftly denied by the Kremlin amid increasing unease over the militarization of space. Tomas Nagy, a senior research fellow at GLOBSEC, a Slovakia-based security think tank, told RFE/RL that evidence of Russia developing a space-capable nuclear weapon remains patchy, but if such a weapon has been developed it could disable swaths of satellites, including the Starlink constellation. "It would not necessarily destroy every satellite, but it would be indiscriminate: Western, Russian, Chinese, and other spacecraft could all be affected by the destructive power of physics and radiation," he said. The impact of a high-altitude nuclear blast comes primarily from the electromagnetic pulse (EMP) that spreads from a nuclear explosion at the speed of light, frying electrical systems in its path. Subsequent radiation in orbit can further degrade delicate satellite components. Victoria Samson , chief director of space security and stability at the Secure World Foundation, a US-based nonprofit, says that in the case of a high-altitude nuclear detonation, mass numbers of satellites within line of sight of the blast would be damaged or completely disabled. “Most satellites are not hardened against nuclear radiation and so if you get your internet from Starlink, for example, that would probably not be an option in this circumstance,” she told RFE/RL. Ukraine is heavily reliant on the American Starlink system for its battlefield coordination amid Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion. On the ground, the same electromagnetic pulse would devastate electrical systems across vast swaths of territory with unknown results. Both the US and Soviet Union detonated powerful nuclear weapons in space during tests in 1962 that caused unforeseen damage on the ground and led to bans on further tests America’s most powerful high altitude nuclear test, codenamed Starfish Prime, occurred on July 9, 1962 some 400 kilometers above the Pacific Ocean. On the American islands of Hawaii, more than 1,200 kilometers away from the blast, roads were plunged into darkness when streetlights failed, air raid sirens spontaneously began to howl, and hundreds of burglar alarms went off across Honolulu. Several of the dozens of satellites in orbit at the time were damaged or disabled by the blast, including the UK's first satellite, Ariel 1. Months later, inside the Soviet Union, scientists looking out at the skies over Soviet Kazakhstan witnessed what one observer described as “a second sun” that briefly blazed overhead. The flash came from a Soviet nuclear weapons test designed to study the effects of high-altitude explosions on missile defenses and communications systems. The bomb was 20 times more powerful than the one that devastated Hiroshima. Observers on the Kazakh steppes felt nothing and heard no explosion but the bomb’s instantaneous electromagnetic pulse devastated electrical systems in the area. Power lines sparked and burned out, their cables falling to the ground , and a fire broke out inside a power station. The electromagnetic blast also disabled a power cable buried around a meter underground that ran electricity between two cities. Many other impacts of the Soviet EMP tests have never been disclosed. In 1963, the Partial Nuclear Test Ban treaty, which prohibited the detonation of nuclear weapons in space was ratified by the US, UK, and USSR, a later treaty banned their placement in orbit. Today, it remains unclear what such a weapon would do to modern infrastructure that is vastly more reliant on delicate electronic systems than that of the 1960s, and to the thousands of active satellites orbiting the Earth today. “Basically if we were to have another Starfish Prime today, we would see even more of an impact in lower Earth orbit because there are so many more satellites there and they are so much more based on electronical components than they were in the 1960s,” Samson said. A 2010 report on the likely damage caused to satellites from an EMP attack concluded that “uncertainties as large as one to two orders of magnitude are postulated” due to a lack of modern data on EMPs. At a recent summit in New York, American weapons manufacturer Palmer Luckey called for the resumption of nuclear testing in large part to research the impact of EMPs on modern infrastructure. He pointed to the archaic data collected during nuclear weapons testing that ended decades ago. "We don't actually know what will happen to our phones, to our critical infrastructure, to our military," in the event of an EMP attack, he said. Amos Chapple is a New Zealand-born writer and visual journalist with a particular interest in the former U.S.S.R.

Two Libyan soldiers have died from injuries sustained in an attack, claimed by Ukraine, on Russian ships near Benghazi, a senior figure in the administration in eastern Libya said late on Tuesday.

Libya is divided between a UN-recognized government in Tripoli and a parallel administration in the east of the country, backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar.

His son Saddam Haftar, who is widely seen as heir apparent, said "it is with deep sadness and great pride that I pay tribute today to two heroes of our naval forces," following the attack.

They "were martyred as a result of their injuries sustained during the performance of their national duty following the criminal attack on the Benghazi Naval Base", he added on Facebook.
